query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Under high shear load during sliding wear, the coarse-grained surface of an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy dynamically transforms into an ultra‐nanocrystalline amorphous layer that exhibits inverse Hall‐Petch behavior, thereby reducing effective shear strength and lowering friction and wear rates.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited, coarse-grained equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy protective coating.
generation.intervention: Conduct sliding wear tests while systematically varying the applied load (from low to high) to induce different levels of shear stress on the coating.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature sliding wear experiments in a controlled environment (preferably ultra-high vacuum or an inert atmosphere to minimize oxidation interference) with loads chosen to straddle the threshold for shear-induced amorphization.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formation of a dynamic, ultra‐nanocrystalline amorphous surface layer generated by severe plastic deformation and heating under high shear conditions.
generation.mechanism: At sufficiently high shear loads, localized plastic deformation and transient temperature spikes trigger a dynamic transformation of the coarse-grained surface into an amorphous layer with extremely fine (2–3 nm) grains. This transformation leads to inverse Hall-Petch behavior where the refined structure exhibits lower shear strength relative to the original coarse-grained state, thus reducing friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings subjected to high load conditions will show clear evidence of a newly formed ultra‐nanocrystalline amorphous layer (as confirmed by TEM) concomitant with reduced friction coefficients and lower wear rates when compared to coatings under low load conditions that retain a coarse-grained structure.
generation.baseline: Coatings tested under low shear loads that do not induce dynamic amorphization, retaining their initial coarse-grained microstructure, higher friction coefficients, and higher wear rates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold over a range of sliding loads typical for wear-resistant applications in HEA coatings, but may not apply if the coating is pre-refined to a nanocrystalline structure or when environmental factors (such as oxidation) dominate the wear behavior.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty in precisely delineating the load threshold for triggering dynamic amorphization and in fully decoupling the effect from potential environmental influences. The replication of the phenomenon across different HEA compositions also remains to be rigorously tested.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform sliding wear tests on as-deposited coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi coatings varying the applied load across a range that includes sub-threshold and super-threshold values. After testing, use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to characterize the near-surface microstructure and measure friction coefficients and wear rates.
measurements: TEM imaging to determine the presence and grain size of any amorphous/nanocrystalline layers
Friction coefficient data recorded during sliding wear
Wear rate measurements from the test wear tracks
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, upon increasing the applied load beyond the predicted threshold, there is no observable formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline amorphous layer and if friction coefficients and wear rates remain comparable to the low-load baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. In the present context of sliding contacts, dynamic amorphization refers to the continuous shear-induced generation of a structurally amorphous layer that accommodates deformation. This is in competition with stress- and temperature-driven grain growth and recrystallization, all of which reestablish crystallinity and order in the shear layer. The shear layer must be amorphized again in subsequent contact passes, thus we refer to this process as dynamic amorphization.

This work studied an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy that was manufactured using a laser-based consolidation additive manufacturing process. We showed that low friction and high wear resistance are achievable with bare high entropy alloys in inert environments. These characteristics are linked to the shear-induced formation of a highly refined, near-amorphous surface film that exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior. The detrimental role of environments, specifically those that result in oxidation, was mitigated by tribological testing in a UHV environment. A newly proposed amorphization model was used to accurately predict the grain size-dependent shear strength, and thus friction coefficient.

proposals.intervention: Perform sliding wear tests under different controlled oxygen partial pressures
proposals.conditions: Room-temperature sliding wear tests in atmospheres ranging from ultra‐high vacuum to controlled oxygen atmospheres (e.g., 0.1 atm O2), keeping other parameters constant (load, speed, humidity)
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation (or suppression) of a nanocrystalline oxide tribolayer on the surface
proposals.mechanism: Selective oxidation during wear promotes the development of a protective, ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer that lowers shear strength and inhibits material removal; the degree of oxide formation is dictated by oxygen availability
proposals.predicted_outcome: Under higher oxygen partial pressures a measurable, continuous nanocrystalline oxide layer forms, resulting in lower wear rates and friction coefficients relative to tests in inert or vacuum environments. The effect should hold over a range of sliding speeds typical of wear-resistant applications.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This hypothesis directly links the controlled surface oxidation state to wear performance by associating the formation of a beneficial tribolayer with reduced wear. A controlled change (oxygen availability) distinguishes the hypothesis from a baseline where oxidation is absent, and clear directional wear-rate differences are expected.

proposals.material_system: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi coating with initial coarse-grained microstructure
proposals.intervention: Subject coatings to variable sliding-induced shear loads in wear tests
proposals.conditions: Sliding wear experiments conducted at room temperature with systematically varied load levels (e.g., low, medium, high load) in ambient air
proposals.structural_mediator: Development of a dynamic, ultra‐nanocrystalline amorphous surface layer generated by shear-induced structural transformation
proposals.mechanism: Under high shear stress, localized temperature rises and plastic deformation trigger dynamic amorphization and nanocrystallization at the surface, thereby reducing effective shear strength and friction; if the applied load exceeds a threshold, an amorphous (and then nanocrystalline) phase forms that is resistant to further wear
proposals.predicted_outcome: At higher loads, in situ formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline amorphous surface layer is observed via high-resolution microscopy along with a reduction in friction coefficient and a lower wear rate compared to lower loads where the layer is absent. This behavior should be consistent over a variety of tested loads representative of operational conditions.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It posits a specific mechanistic role for dynamic amorphization as the governing factor in wear performance by linking in situ shear-induced structural transformations to wear resistance. The controlled variable (load/shear stress) distinguishes the mechanism from a baseline without dynamic layering, and clear transformational markers (layer appearance, friction drop) can be verified.

proposals.material_system: CoCrFeMnNi coating with varied thermal annealing treatments
proposals.intervention: Apply post-deposition thermal annealing at carefully controlled temperatures to tailor surface grain size
proposals.conditions: Thermal annealing at different temperatures (e.g., 500°C, 700°C, 900°C) in inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, followed by standard sliding wear tests at room temperature
proposals.structural_mediator: Grain size refinement at the surface and in near-surface regions, influencing grain boundary density
proposals.mechanism: According to an inverse Hall-Petch effect, reducing grain size (increasing grain boundary area) under certain nanoscale dimensions can decrease the shear strength of the surface, thus improving energy dissipation during wear; tuning the grain size should modulate wear rates
proposals.predicted_outcome: Coatings with finer, controlled grain sizes (achieved via moderate annealing) exhibit lower wear rates and friction coefficients compared to as-deposited or coarser-grained coatings. There is an optimal grain size range within which wear resistance is maximized; deviations (excessively fine or large grains) would show inferior performance.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This path tests a mechanical hypothesis where the microstructural grain boundary characteristics directly govern wear performance. The controlled change (annealing temperature leading to different grain sizes) and its expected correlation with wear properties allow differentiation from a baseline microstructure.

proposals.material_system: CrMnFeCoNi-based HEA coating with controlled additions of carbide-forming elements (e.g., ZrC)
proposals.intervention: Incorporate varying small fractions of ZrC into the HEA coating via magnetron sputtering or plasma transferred arc process
proposals.conditions: Prepare a series of coatings with ZrC contents ranging from 0 to 4 wt% under identical deposition conditions; perform wear tests in ambient atmosphere at room temperature
proposals.structural_mediator: Precipitation or dispersion of fine, uniformly distributed second-phase ZrC particles within the HEA matrix
proposals.mechanism: The presence of a finely dispersed hard secondary phase is hypothesized to arrest fatigue crack initiation and propagation during sliding contact, thereby imparting improved toughness and enhanced wear resistance. Even though prior work showed ZrC impacting hardness and corrosion performance, careful microstructural control might reveal its role in wear behavior when tuned appropriately.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Coatings with an optimal ZrC content (near a threshold value) will display a quantifiable decrease in wear rate and friction coefficient relative to pure HEA coatings under the same test conditions. Outside this optimal content, either insufficient pinning or interface degradation may lead to performance similar to the baseline.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach focuses on an alloying/dispersion mechanism that could govern wear performance by modifying the microstructural landscape. The controlled addition of ZrC provides a clear variable that, if influencing wear resistance via second-phase hardening mechanisms, would be distinguishable from coatings lacking such engineered particle dispersions.

decision.rationale: Direction C directly tests a mechanism supported by several studies where high shear loads induce dynamic amorphization leading to the formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline amorphous surface layer. This mechanism, observed in CoCrFeMnNi HEAs under sliding wear in environments that minimize oxidation, is strongly supported by evidence (e.g., PMC7311485) and offers a clear, load‐dependent change from the baseline. In contrast, while directions A, B, and D each propose mechanisms related to wear, direction A has been shown to have limited impact on wear improvement in previous work, B involves a thermal post-treatment that creates static (rather than dynamic) microstructural features, and D depends on oxidation effects that can complicate interpretation. Thus, we adopt direction C as the most directly testable mechanistic hypothesis.
